newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE-Snakes, crashes may bring lotto luck in Malaysia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Snakes, crashes may bring lotto luck in Malaysia.

text.p: It's 6.30 p.m. on a Sunday, and a steady stream of people shuffle into a brightly lit, four-digit lottery shop in Kuala Lumpur.
They stop, and gaze ponderously at the numbers scrawled on white boards around the shop, adorned with posters of surprised models surrounded by wads of cash, luxury cars, and houses.

Having consulted numerology books and their dreams -- even those about reptiles and car crashes -- they take printed betting slips, choose four numbers and hand them over to cashiers behind glass counters along with their bet.
The scene is similar in hundreds of other betting shops across Malaysia, which officially is Moslem but where all sorts of gambling thrive.
Three times a week, on Saturdays, Sundays and Wednesdays, Magnum Corporation Bhd and Berjaya Sports Toto, a division of the Berjaya Group, publish their lottery results.

Olympia Industries runs a popular lottery in the Borneo state of Sabah. Other listed gaming concerns include blue chip counters Genting Bhd and Resorts World, which run casinos, and horse-track betting operator Tanjong Plc.
SPECIAL DREAMS HELP
CHOOSE NUMBERS

"I do it (place bets) only when I get a special dream," said Anand, owner of an instant rubber stamp-making business. On this day, he is betting his car registration number and those of his two brothers' national identification cards.
He bets a total of 10 ringgit ($4) and could win anything up to 10,800 ringgit ($4,355).

Mary, a Chinese woman in her late 40s, sits at the back of her Berjaya Sports Toto shop in the grimy, noisy Pudu area of central Kuala Lumpur. A Chinese customer walks in and asks if the jackpot is still standing. It is -- at just under one million ringgit ($400,000).
With stakes like these, it's easy to see why some punters bet big. "Some come in here and spend around 2,000 ringgit ($800) each time," Mary said.
It is also clear why listed companies like Magnum are constantly on the "buy" lists of several regional fund managers.
According to Shirley Tey, gaming analyst at equities research house H.G. Asia in Kuala Lumpur, Magnum alone paid out about 1.9 billion ringgit ($766 million) in prize money in 1996.
PREDOMINANTLY MOSLEM COUNTRY
What makes these statistics surprising is that Malaysia is a predominantly Moslem country. All forms of gambling are strictly forbidden under Islam.

Although more than 40 percent of the population are Chinese, Indian and other non-Moslem groups, a surprising number of ethnic Moslem Malays bet regularly. On this Sunday night, which also happens to fall in the holy fasting month of Ramadan, a good proportion of the punters look distinctly Malay.
But the lotteries contribute a hefty amount to state coffers and it is highly unlikely the government would want to kill them off, analysts said.

Most punters have their own system for choosing numbers, ranging from combinations of birthdays and anniversaries to the A local cameraman said he saw a woman approach the winner of a children's talent contest and ask the girl to give her four numbers. "I thought she was getting the girl's autograph," he said.

Several punters spoke of books containing numerological guides to everyday objects, animals and events. Any of the objects appearing in a dream are supposed to be lucky and should therefore bring luck if bet on.
For example, snakes are denoted by the number 606, accidents by 408.
Last year when a newspaper printed a front-page story and picture of a python that had killed and nearly swallowed a man, combinations of snake number 606 sold out within hours, local punters said.

Drivers on Malaysian roads are familiar with infuriating traffic jams caused by people slowing down to gawk at accidents -- not out of a macabre sense of curiosity but to write down the number plates of the cars involved.
"The numbers are bad for the accident people, but not for the passersby," Mary said.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 4813)
